title: 🎥 Come and See — The Film That Made Me Question Why I Even Watch Movies

commenti.body: i moreso mean the fact that your obviously just using ai to write these comments

Yeah man, fair call. I’m 18 and I’ve logged around 300 films on Letterboxd, so I’m still figuring out my taste. Most of what I’ve seen leans toward stylized stuff—anime, thrillers, emotional dramas with clear arcs. Come and See was just..a lot. I get why it’s powerful, but it didn’t click with me the way it does for others.

I haven’t watched many hyper-realistic or war films yet, so maybe I wasn’t ready for how raw and chaotic it is. My reaction wasn’t meant to dismiss it, just being honest about where I’m at. My taste doesn’t match this kind of film yet, and I know that’s on me more than the movie.

Appreciate the pushback though it’s helping me see things from a wider perspective.I’ll probably revisit it down the line with more context under my belt.

You're allowed to trash the film, hate it, and do so as bluntly as you like. Read the Letterbox reviews for *Come and See* and you'll get a lot of people who sit with you on this. 

Aside from the fact that this isn't Letterboxd and you need something slightly more analytical than "I just didn't enjoy this movie" to justify posting it, I think like someone else here said it seems like maybe you've not seen a whole lot of films before watching this one because you've confused a very slight deviation from tradition to be an abandonment of all that is cinema.

It's not about you being real or fitting in, all the comments here said it's totally fine to not like the movie or to feel numb or to feel however anyone feels watching it. The thing is, you talked about your personal feelings but also about the complete lack of value of the movie's craft, which is what everyone here disagreed with, and for very good reasons. The film is formally excellent, and not particularly out there in regard to its storytelling and structure techniques.

I get why it might come off that way online takes can feel recycled half the time. But this one’s mine, start to finish. I sat with the film, let it mess with me, and tried to put that into words as honestly as I could. No templates, no borrowed phrasing, just me trying to make sense of what I felt.  

I know it’s not the popular take, and I’m not here to chase karma. I write because some films demand a response that’s personal, even if it’s clumsy or raw. If it sounds too polished, maybe that’s just how I process things tight language doesn’t mean it’s not real.  

Appreciate the callout though. Keeps the space honest. But yeah, this one’s all me

Okay, maybe I came off a little too blunt in my take. I wasn’t trying to trash the film.it just didn’t hit me the way it clearly hit others. I get that Come and See is a masterpiece for a lot of people. I respect that.  

But when I watched it, I didn’t feel devastated or enlightened. I felt weirdly numb. And I don’t know if that’s a failure on my part or the film’s, or maybe that’s exactly what it wanted. Either way, I wasn’t trying to be edgy.I was just being honest.  

If that earns me downvotes, fair. But I’d rather be real than pretend I had a spiritual awakening just to fit in.

Dude I'm not shouting at you, I'm just furthering our discussion. But I have to say this:

>For me, the film’s power comes despite its structure, not because of it. The aesthetic is there, but it’s so warped and destabilized that I found it hard to engage emotionally. I respect what it’s doing, but it didn’t land for me the way it clearly did for others.

Is very different from this:

>But from a film-as-craft perspective? It lacks everything

You could have save yourself so much time by just not enjoying the movie - I say with zero condescension that that's totally fine, it's not a fun hang.

This is beautifully put and I think you’re onto something essential with the idea of intentional refusal. That’s a much more compelling way to frame what I initially called “lack of craft.” You’re right-it’s not absence, it’s weaponized incompleteness. The film denies us rhythm and payoff because it’s not trying to soothe,it’s trying to rupture.

I also love the “third register” idea. Grave of the Fireflies devastates through empathy, Shoah through testimony, and Come and See through sensory collapse. That  makes me rethink my own reaction. Maybe I was expecting narrative scaffolding where Klimov was offering psychic erosion.

I still wrestle with how it landed for me emotionally it felt more numbing than immersive,but I completely respect the argument that it’s cinema as witness, not story. And maybe that’s why it unsettled me so much: it didn’t ask me to watch, it asked me to absorb.

Appreciate this take.It’s the kind of reply that makes me rethink my own review.

Oh I very much disagree. You're right about the rawness and the dream collapsing aspects of the film, but I completely disagree with your assessment of the whole movie.

I can understand your personal tastes not fitting Come and See. It's absolutely not for everyone and I can perfectly see how the themes and brutality of the movie will just be off-putting even for some people who are very much into movies.

But what I personally believe you're wrong with is the "It lacks everything from a film-as-craft perspective". The film has basically everything I understand as valuable from that same perspective:

- Absolute dedication to its theme.
- Powerful storytelling and structure that provide an original and strong point of view to a played out setting.
- Thought-out main character arc. It's more "show, don't tell" than others, but the MC has a clearly defined traditional arc.
- Devastating emotional rhythm. I can't understand why would you say there isn't any.
- Great visual formal rigor.
- Outstanding mise-en-scene.
- Fantastic acting.

This post really just says you need to watch more films. Come and See is not unique in that aspect. It still has a structure, it is still linear, it is still plot-heavy. 

Many films have little to none of those things. Come and See really isn’t out on its own in the aspects you mentioned. It’s a great film with a lot of weight but get out there and watch some truly avant-garde stuff and then come back to it and it will seem a lot more straightforward.
Having an opinion is one thing, but at least write them yourself

I really appreciate the depth of your argument and you're right to highlight how Klimov’s choices are deliberate and rooted in cinematic tradition. I don’t mean to suggest he’s just pointing a camera at horror. My “exit from the cinematic conversation” line was more about how Come and See feels like it’s operating on a different emotional frequency than most films it’s not trying to guide the viewer, it’s trying to overwhelm them.

That said, I still stand by my take. For me, the film’s power comes despite its structure, not because of it. The aesthetic is there, but it’s so warped and destabilized that I found it hard to engage emotionally. I respect what it’s doing, but it didn’t land for me the way it clearly did for others.

I think we’re just rating different things and that’s okay. I’m glad this film provokes such strong reactions. That’s a sign of something real.

What’s fascinating about *Come and See* is that it almost weaponizes the absence of craft you mention. The lack of rhythm, payoff, or catharsis isn’t a failure of storytelling - it’s an intentional refusal. Made in the mid-80s, it arrives at a time when the Soviet Union was beginning to rethink its own war mythology. In that sense, the “incompleteness” isn’t a flaw but part of the film’s historical position: it’s cinema refusing to give its audience a traditional narrative to hide inside.

When you compare it to something like *Grave of the Fireflies*, which is devastating because of its emotional rhythm, or *Shoah*, which devastates through duration and testimony, *Come and See* feels like it’s working in a third register: a purely sensory destabilization. The sound design, the distortions of perspective, even the actor’s gaze into the camera - they collapse the safe distance that most films maintain.

I think that’s why people call it a masterpiece. Not because it’s “enjoyable,” or even narratively satisfying, but because it dares to ask whether cinema can serve as testimony rather than story.

So maybe the real question isn’t “is it good cinema?” but “what do we want cinema to do?” Should it console us with craft, or disturb us with witness?

My point was that Klimov achieved both; quoth:

>The fact that Kilmov manages with without entirely throwing away moments of **formally well-made and directed sequences, interesting and dynamic choices as a director, and, as I said, a kind of warped narrative structure,** all within the confines of the Soviet film industry, is even more power to him.

*Come and See* is not documentary-style filmmaking (like Paul Greengrass) or an attempt at objectivity, so I find it really odd to say that Klimov "exits the cinematic conversation". There are and were plenty of auteurs making the same sort of directorial choices he made (especially European directors) and sans those choices (as I said) the movie would be different altogether. We are firmly in Florya's subjective experience as a result of everything Klimov choices to do as a director from the bottom up; he's not pointing and shooting atrocities like a Mondo film. 

Invoking very strong sensations =/= an abdication of aesthetic

Appreciate the thoughtful pushback—this is exactly the kind of discourse Come and See provokes, and I respect that you see it as the definitive cinematic reckoning with WWII. I don’t disagree with its historical weight or its raw power. But I think we’re rating two different things.

You’re evaluating it as a document of horror, and in that sense, yeah—it’s unmatched. The chaos, the dread, the psychological collapse—it’s visceral and unflinching. But I came at it from a film-as-craft lens. And from that angle, it felt like Kilmov intentionally abandoned the grammar of cinema to make something more primal. That’s bold, but it also means it doesn’t function like a film in the traditional sense. It’s not about payoff -it’s about corrosion.

The “molested hero’s journey” idea is fascinating, and I see where you’re coming from. But for me, Florya isn’t journeying—he’s dissolving. There’s no arc, just entropy. And while that’s thematically potent, it didn’t emotionally land for me. It felt like I was watching trauma through a fogged lens disturbing, yes, but not immersive.

Also, totally agree on Zone of Interest vs Schindler’s List that’s a brilliant contrast. But I’d argue Come and See is so singular it almost exits the cinematic conversation entirely. It’s not trying to be a film—it’s trying to be a scream. And that’s why I gave it a 5/10—not as a dismissal, but as an acknowledgment that it broke the scale I usually rate by.

If you truly felt it "lacked everything", maybe you should question at least what films you want to see. Not everything is about a neat 3 act story or an emotional payoff. See enough films and these wont matter at all.

Well, there's no accounting for taste I suppose.

Without going too deeply into your assertion that it lacks structure, emotional rhythm, or payoff (I'd disagree with all of these; the structure almost feels like some sort of molested hero's journey, it's pulsating with rhytym, and if the director hadn't had such a strong presence, we'd be watching something totally different) --

*Come And See* is, imo (and this is a hot take, I know) the only cinematic representation of the true horrors of WW2 put on film. For example, very Holocaust movie in one way or another never rises above the primary trappings of cinematic aesthetic (*Zone of Interest* goes in the other direction, interestingly, and constructs almost a secondary film about the Holocaust that is never literally depicted on screen; *Schindler's List* is sad and sometimes graphically tragic but still with a Spielberg sheen). *Come and See* is probably the closest you'd come, as a person removed in time and space, in capturing the actual chaos and unyielding fear and anxiety of surviving a genocidal war (I'd consider what happened in Belarus genocide, without getting into politics).

The fact that Kilmov manages with without entirely throwing away moments of formally well-made and directed sequences, interesting and dynamic choices as a director, and, as I said, a kind of warped narrative structure, all within the confines of the Soviet film industry, is even more power to him.
